subject: history

moments.title: Hippocratic medicine
moments.body: The Hippocratic corpus — around 60 texts attributed to Hippocrates and his followers — proposes natural rather than supernatural causes of disease, and introduces the four humours: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile. The Hippocratic Oath (probably 5th century BCE) shapes medical ethics for two millennia.
moments.takeaway: Disease as imbalance of bodily fluids ruled medical thinking until Pasteur's germ theory (1860s).

moments.title: Galen synthesises
moments.who: Galen of Pergamon, physician to Marcus Aurelius
moments.body: Galen writes massively — perhaps 500 treatises. He systematises humoural theory, dissects animals (human dissection was forbidden in Rome), and treats wounded gladiators. His Anatomical Procedures and On the Natural Faculties become the canonical medical texts.
moments.takeaway: Galen's authority lasted 1,400 years — sustained partly because his Christian readers approved of his teleological natural philosophy.

moments.title: Galen unchallenged
moments.body: Galen's works were preserved in Greek and translated into Arabic (Hunayn ibn Ishaq, 9th century). Avicenna's Canon (1025) synthesised Galenic medicine with Aristotelian philosophy and dominated European medical schools through to Vesalius.
moments.takeaway: For over 1,000 years, Galen was 'the Physician' — to challenge him was to challenge medicine itself.

now.title: What we kept and what we abandoned
now.body: Modern medicine rejects the four humours. But fragments persist: melancholy and choleric as temperaments, 'humours' as moods, the Hippocratic Oath (in updated form) at medical school graduations. Acupuncture, Ayurveda and other ancient systems remain in use, with mixed evidence bases.
now.open_questions: Why did humoural medicine work as well as it sometimes did? Bed rest, herbal preparations and dietary advice produced real benefits for some conditions, independent of theoretical justification.

reflection: Medical knowledge is cumulative but not linear. The framework that ruled for two millennia turned out to be wrong in its fundamentals — but the practitioners and patients who used it were not foolish. Each era's medicine is the best its conceptual tools allow.
